floors.content: Put a number into the rule "double it and add three." The rule does not care which number is chosen.
If 2 goes in, 7 comes out. If 5 goes in, 13 comes out. Each input is handled the same way.
A function is a rule that takes an allowed input and returns a definite output, with no guessing in between.
The same function can be written in words, in a table, on a graph, or as a formula, depending on what is easiest to read.
The pairing is the thing to watch: each input is sent to its own output, and that pairing is the function.
Take the rule "double it and add three" and try it on several input numbers, one after another, without changing the rule.
Each input-output pair becomes a point. The input gives the x-position, and the output gives the y-position on the plane.
When the points for 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 are plotted, they form an ordered pattern rather than scattered marks.
For this rule, the points fall on a straight line because the output rises by the same amount each time.
A graph is the rule placed on the plane, where its pattern can be seen instead of only calculated from a table.
A ramp can rise gently or sharply, and each step covers horizontal distance while the height changes by some amount.
On a graph, slope measures a similar comparison: how much y changes when x changes by a chosen amount along the horizontal axis.
If x moves one step right while y rises two steps, the slope is two for that line throughout its length.
Slope is not merely a drawing feature on the page. It is a rate of change inside the line itself.
The same idea will later measure speed, growth, reaction rate, and other changing quantities that compare one change with another.
Put time along the x-axis and position along the y-axis. Now the graph can describe motion instead of only numbers.
A flat line means the position is not changing, so the object is sitting still during that stretch of time.
A rising straight line means the object is moving steadily away from the starting position as time passes on the graph.
The slope of that line is the velocity, because it tells how position changes with time in each equal interval.
A line that once described a number rule can also describe a moving object as its position changes over time.
Push a toy car across the floor, and the car can now do things it could not do before the push.
It can roll into a block, climb a small ramp, or scrape along the floor until friction slows it down.
Energy is the account used for the ability to produce motion, heat, lifting, stretching, or some other physical change in matter.
Energy is not a liquid inside the car, but it can be transferred from one object or process to another.
A rolling car, a warm floor, and a lifted weight can be connected by following where the energy transfers during each event.
Push a box across the floor. The push changes the box only while the box moves through some distance across the surface.
A person can push against a wall and become tired, even though the wall has not moved through any measurable distance.
In physics, work means a force acting through a distance in the same direction as the motion of the object.
A force alone is not enough, and motion alone is not enough. The force has to act through the motion.
In the simplest case, work is written as W = Fd: force multiplied by distance in the direction of motion on the object.
A tennis ball and a bowling ball can roll at the same speed, but stopping them requires very different pushes.
The bowling ball carries more motion to deal with because the same speed is attached to much more mass than the tennis ball.
Momentum is mass times velocity, so it depends on both the amount of matter and the direction of motion, not speed alone.
Because velocity has direction, momentum has direction too. It points in the same direction as the moving object travels through space.
Momentum becomes important in collisions, recoils, explosions, and pushes between objects that act on each other during contact or separation.
Catching a fast ball with stiff hands can hurt because the stop happens quickly and the force becomes large on the hands.
Moving the hands backward during the catch makes the same ball easier to handle during the stop because the stopping time increases.
The ball's momentum still changes, but the change is spread over a longer time instead of one sudden jolt through the hands.
Impulse is force multiplied by time, and it equals the change in momentum during a push, collision, or stop between objects.
Gloves, airbags, mats, and crumple zones all use the same principle: stretch the stop so the force becomes smaller at impact.
Iron left outside in rain changes over time, and the shiny metal begins to rust on the surface as oxygen reacts.
The iron has not vanished. Its atoms have joined with oxygen from the air to make a new substance on the metal.
A chemical reaction rearranges atoms. It does not make the atoms disappear from the material world; it changes their connections.
The starting substances are reactants. The substances formed afterward are products of the same rearrangement of atoms across the reaction.
Chemistry keeps count of which atoms were present before and where those atoms ended up after the reaction in the products.
If a reaction begins with six carbon atoms, the products must still contain six carbon atoms afterward on the product side.
The atoms may be rearranged into new molecules, but the count of each element is preserved through the reaction rather than destroyed.
Balancing a chemical equation is atom bookkeeping: count before, count after, then adjust whole molecules until the counts match on both sides.
The number of molecules can change, but the formula inside a molecule is not edited during balancing because that changes the substance.
The equation is balanced when every element has the same count on both sides of the reaction arrow after adjustment.
Strike a match, and the reaction gives off heat and light almost immediately from the flame as substances change inside the match head.
The atoms are rearranging, and energy is being transferred to the surroundings as heat and light during the reaction in the flame.
Some reactions release energy and warm the surroundings. Other reactions absorb energy and lower the nearby temperature during the process.
Chemical bonds belong in the energy account, because breaking and making bonds changes stored energy in the reacting substances inside molecules.
Chemistry tracks atoms, but it also tracks the energy moving with those atoms during a reaction as bonds change and products form.
Lemon juice tastes sharp because its molecules behave as acids when they dissolve and interact with water in the mouth.
A first model of an acid is a substance that can give away hydrogen ions when dissolved in water during reactions.
A hydrogen ion is basically a proton, so acids are often described as proton donors in many reactions in solution.
That picture will need refining later, but it already explains many common acid reactions that happen in water as proton transfers.
A tiny charged particle moving from one molecule to another can change the behaviour of a whole solution by shifting charge.
Computer memory can be pictured as a long hallway of numbered lockers, each holding a small piece of information at an address.
To read the right locker, the computer needs an address, not a vague description of where the value might be.
Memory works like this: stored values live in numbered places the machine can point to directly instead of searching by description.
A program can ask for the value at an address, change it, or use the stored value in a calculation.
Before software does anything large, the machine is already doing a lot of careful pointing between addresses and values while it runs.
Stack plates in a cupboard, and the last plate placed on top is the first one removed from the pile.
Computers use a similar idea when a program enters a function and later returns from it in the right order.
The stack remembers short-lived information: where to return, local values, and unfinished work for the current function call inside the program.
When the function finishes, its stack space is cleared, like removing the top plate from the pile above it during return.
The stack lets a program enter a smaller job, finish it, and return to the larger job without losing its place.
A long message sent across a network usually does not travel as one huge lump from start to finish across machines.
It is broken into smaller packets, each carrying data and information about where it should go across the network toward its destination.
Packets can travel through different routes, arrive out of order, and still be reassembled into the message at the end.
This makes networks flexible, because one broken path does not have to stop the whole message from moving through another route.
The internet is less like one pipe and more like a postal system for small numbered pieces moving between machines.
A website name is easy for humans to remember, but machines need a more exact destination on the network before sending data.
The network cannot send a request to "the site I meant." It needs an address that points to a machine.
DNS is the lookup system that turns a name like example.com into an address machines can use for routing.
Without DNS, web addresses would work more like memorised phone numbers than human-readable names for every site on the network.
DNS is one of the translation layers that hides the addressing system underneath ordinary website names used by machines during lookup.
A balanced chemical equation, a momentum collision, and a computer memory address look unrelated at first because their objects differ.
All three depend on keeping track of what goes where during a change from one state to another without losing count.
Chemistry tracks atoms, physics tracks quantities like energy and momentum, and computing tracks values in memory as systems change over time.
Mathematics supplies the language for that tracking: numbers, rules, graphs, and equations for comparing quantities across different systems and changes.
The subjects separate on the surface, then meet again when the counting becomes serious across different problems, materials, and motions.
A slope on a graph, a car's velocity, a reaction rate, and network speed share the same mathematical skeleton despite different labels.
Each one compares a change in something with a change in something else over the same interval of time or distance.
Position per time gives velocity. Product formed per time gives reaction rate. Data per time gives bandwidth in a network.
Mathematics gives the reusable pattern, and each science attaches that pattern to a different situation without changing the underlying structure.
Rate is one of the places where the subjects use the same tool under different names across different fields and contexts.
A falling ball, a burning match, and a glowing screen all ask the same question about energy during change across different processes.
The central question is where the energy came from, where it went, and what changed while it moved between forms.
In physics, energy changes between height, motion, heat, sound, and other forms during events such as falls, collisions, and heating.
In chemistry, energy is tied to bonds breaking and forming during reactions between atoms in molecules and materials as products form.
In computing, electrical energy is spent moving charge through circuits and switching transistors on and off inside processors many times.
Drop an effervescent tablet into cold water, and the bubbles appear slowly at first around the tablet as gas forms.
Drop the same kind of tablet into warm water, and the fizz usually becomes faster almost immediately as particle motion increases.
The reaction is similar, but the speed of the reaction has changed because the conditions changed inside the water around the tablet.
A reaction rate measures how quickly reactants turn into products during a chemical change over a measured time in a system.
Chemistry often asks what will form, and also how fast that product will form under the chosen conditions during a reaction.
